channel.title: Protocol STAMP
channel.description: An independent program that measures whether an AI can be made to show its receipts. Issues on alternate Saturdays at 15:37 America/Chicago; The Bench on Mondays and Thursdays. Protocol STAMP can make mistakes; verify before you implement anything, and see https://protocolstamp.com/corrections/ for what we have already got wrong.

item.title: The Bench Vol 006 · A Name Is Not a Test
item.description: The US renamed AI “Super Intelligence” without changing what the word covers, and the UN talks on autonomous weapons ended without a treaty. Both turn on one question: who checks what an AI is said to be? Why we still write “AI,” where military AI rules reach testing, and what we propose.

item.title: Militaries and AI, country by country
item.description: A new standing page on how armed forces govern AI: the UN talks on autonomous weapons, which ended on Sep 04, 2026 without a treaty; REAIM and the US Political Declaration; NATO; and national policy from the US to Ukraine. 63 references, with seven new Docket and eleven new Chronicle entries.

item.title: Super Intelligence (SI): the US rename of AI, traced
item.description: Executive Order 14434 tells US agencies to write “Super Intelligence” for AI, with the same legal definition. The timeline, who has followed it and who has not, why the term is contested, and why this site still writes “AI.” 37 references.

item.title: The Bench Vol 005 · Judges Who Agree With Each Other
item.description: Our three judges agreed with each other at 0.875 and with one person at 0.631 to 0.685. Nine published studies of AI judges, 2023 to 2026, bear on that and none measured it: what each found, where it reaches our work, and what we propose to take from it, starting with printing four numbers for every judge instead of one.

item.title: The Bench Vol 004 · What a New Judge Has to Beat
item.description: Two decision models went through the seven rules of Vol 003. The agreement bar was met, to three decimal places, by a judge that only ever says PASS, and the rule that asked a person is what stopped them. A proposal for how a new kind of model, Jev or whatever comes next, should be tested here: seven steps, starting with the judge that always says yes.

item.title: The Bench Vol 003 · Five Cases, a Hundred Times Each
item.description: LangChain reported that Jev, a new decision model, matched a human reviewer on all 500 pass/fail decisions it judged. The 500 were five cases repeated a hundred times. What that can carry, the open models that followed, and the seven rules any judge must pass before it grades our work.

item.title: The Bench Vol 002 · Something It Can Actually Check
item.description: Four Claude models were handed a record with two errors planted in it, twice - once with web search off, once with it on. All twelve cells caught both. Retrieval changed nothing about that, and everything about what could honestly be said afterwards.

item.title: The Bench Vol 001 · The No. 1 Complaint
item.description: Is hallucination really what people hate most about AI? The review data says yes. Then thirteen AI models were asked the same question, word for word, and the answer that came back was that our own table was wrong. It was, nine times over.

item.title: Stop marking it like a student
item.description: A model guesses when your question looks like it wants help, and hedges when it looks like it might cause harm. Neither behavior is about what the model knows. Both are about how it is marked.

item.title: Why "I don't know" can be a lie
item.description: Most prompt hygiene guards against invention and stops there. The case for treating abstention as a symmetric failure, and what it costs to guard only one side.
